From inputs to updated weights

Understand an LSTM,
one operation at a time.

What the gates control, how memory survives, how a final error travels backward, and how one complete epoch changes the model.

The worked epoch below starts from the simulation’s default initialization: 1 hidden unit, 30 normal readings, learning rate 0.04, clipping limit 1. Its numbers are recalculated using the same model code as the lecture. Reading the docs does not change your simulation.

1. Start with the task

Our synthetic battery sequence is warning → 30 normal readings → inspection. The target is “Check needed,” even though the recent readings are normal. A healthy control starts with a normal reading and contains no warning. The model must distinguish these sequences by remembering the early event.

There are 32 time steps: the first observation, 30 intervening readings, and the inspection query. The training labels are y = 1 for warning and y = 0 for healthy. This is a simplified precursor-memory task, not a physical battery temperature model.

Encode each event

\sym{x}{x_{\mathrm{warning}}}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \sym{x}{x_{\mathrm{normal}}}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \sym{x}{x_{\mathrm{inspect}}}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}

The positions mean [warning, normal, inspection]. One-hot encoding identifies categories; it does not rank their magnitude. A weight row multiplied by one of these vectors selects the weight for that event.

[w_1,w_2,w_3]\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}=w_1

Each sequence has its own zero initial states. We reuse the same weights across time and across training examples.

2. Read the notation and dimensions

Every underlined notation is interactive, including symbols inside the displayed equations.

Vector model versus our scalar walkthrough

\xt\in\mathbb R^{\sym{D}{D}},\qquad \ht,\ct\in\mathbb R^{\sym{H}{H}}
\W{a}\in\mathbb R^{H\times D},\quad \U{a}\in\mathbb R^{H\times H},\quad \bias{a}\in\mathbb R^H

The input size is D = 3. Hidden size H is configurable from 1 to 4 in the lecture. The worked epoch uses H = 1, so states and gates are scalars. General equations use elementwise multiplication; that is ordinary multiplication in the scalar example.

Time steps are repeated uses of the same recurrent layer. Thirty-two drawn cells do not mean thirty-two independently parameterized layers.

3. Why an LSTM has two state paths

The RNN baseline

a_t=W_r\xt+U_r\hp+b_r,\qquad \ht=\th(a_t)

An RNN combines the new input and its previous hidden state, then recomputes the state through tanh. It has no separate cell-state lane. Our initial RNN notices the warning strongly, but the recurrent multiplier 0.55 weakens its representation through the long normal gap.

h_1=\tanh(2)=0.9640,\qquad h_2=\tanh(0.55h_1)=0.4855

At small states, tanh(z) ≈ z. Repeated multiplication by 0.55 then shrinks the early signal. In this initial example, h₃₂ is approximately 7.63 × 10⁻⁹.

The LSTM alternative

\ct=\gatef\had\cp+\gatei\had\cand,\qquad \ht=\gateo\had\th(\ct)

cₜ is internal memory; hₜ is exposed output and recurrent context. The LSTM can retain a substantial warning in c while exposing a small h. The additive cell-state update gives memory a direct route across time.

What actually stores information?

The cell state c stores the internal memory. The hidden state h is an exposed representation. Forget, input, and output gates are temporary control values calculated at each step; they do not independently store the warning. Candidate g is proposed content.

4. Every gate: equation, intuition, and purpose

For each component a ∈ {f, i, g, o}, first calculate an affine preactivation:

\za=\W{a}\xt+\U{a}\hp+\bias{a}

W applies to the current event. U applies to previous exposed context. The bias is a learned offset. Every component receives the same xₜ and hₜ₋₁; none uses the newly calculated hₜ.

Activations and their derivatives

\sig(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad \sigma'(z)=\sig(z)(1-\sig(z))
\th(z)=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}},\qquad \tanh'(z)=1-\th^2(z)

Sigmoid gives a fraction in (0,1), suitable for controlling an amount. Tanh gives signed content in (−1,1). Saturated activations have small derivatives. Forward values and backward derivatives are related, but they are not the same quantity.

Forget gate: retain old memory

\gatef=\sig(\W{f}\xt+\U{f}\hp+\bias{f})
\mathrm{retained}_t=\gatef\had\cp

Intuition: a tap on the old memory lane. A value near one retains most memory; a value near zero removes most of it.

Purpose: let the model discard obsolete content while preserving useful context. It controls retention; it does not store a separate copy of the event.

Default bias bf = 4 gives f = σ(4) ≈ 0.9820. Repeated retention still decays slightly. Forget gates near one help preserve memory; they do not guarantee perfect retention.

Input gate: admit new content

\gatei=\sig(\W{i}\xt+\U{i}\hp+\bias{i})
\mathrm{written}_t=\gatei\had\cand

Intuition: permission to write. It determines the fraction accepted from the candidate, not the candidate’s meaning.

Purpose: prevent irrelevant readings from overwriting valuable memory. In the initial model, a warning opens this gate to about 0.9820; a normal reading mostly closes it to about 0.0180.

Candidate: propose what could be stored

\cand=\th(\W{g}\xt+\U{g}\hp+\bias{g})

The candidate is also written c̃ₜ. It is a tanh-transformed proposal, not a sigmoid gate and not yet stored memory.

Intuition: write a proposed note, then let the input gate decide how much to accept.

Purpose: learn an internal representation of the event. Initially, the warning produces g = tanh(2) ≈ 0.9640. Normal readings produce g = 0. These values change when training updates the candidate weights.

Cell state: combine retained and accepted content

\boxed{\ct=\gatef\had\cp+\gatei\had\cand}

Intuition: keep part of the old note and add the accepted part of the new note.

Purpose: carry useful information forward without completely recomputing it at every observation. This is where the memory is stored. The full cell-state update is not passed through tanh, so c is not constrained to (−1,1).

Output gate: expose part of the memory

\gateo=\sig(\W{o}\xt+\U{o}\hp+\bias{o})
\boxed{\ht=\gateo\had\th(\ct)}

Intuition: a window onto internal memory. A closed window does not erase what is stored.

Purpose: control how memory affects the next cell’s gate calculations and the final prediction. Tanh squashes a copy of c; it does not replace c. Initially, the inspection token opens the output gate much more than normal readings do.

5. A complete forward pass

Start with c₀ = h₀ = 0. Keep all parameters fixed while processing the entire sequence. Cache each input, prior state, preactivation, gate value, and resulting state: backpropagation will need these values.

Initial LSTM parameters

ComponentInput weights WRecurrent UBias b
Forget[0, 0, 0]04
Input[8, 0, 0]0−4
Candidate[2, 0, 0]00
Output[0, 0, 8]0−4

The readout starts with v = 8 and bᵧ = −1. All recurrent U values start at zero in this illustrative LSTM; they are trainable. The general equations still include them because later updates can make them nonzero.

Time 1: warning enters memory

\begin{aligned}f_1&=\sigma(4)=0.9820\\ i_1&=\sigma(8-4)=0.9820\\ g_1&=\tanh(2)=0.9640\\ o_1&=\sigma(-4)=0.0180\end{aligned}
c_1=f_1c_0+i_1g_1=0.9820(0)+0.9820(0.9640)=0.9467
h_1=o_1\tanh(c_1)=0.01328

A large c and small h are perfectly consistent: the warning is stored internally, while little of it is exposed.

Time 2: a normal reading arrives

f_2=0.9820,\quad i_2=0.0180,\quad g_2=0,\quad o_2=0.0180
c_2=0.9820(0.9467)+0.0180(0)=0.9297,\quad h_2=0.01314

The normal reading initially adds zero candidate content. Most stored memory survives.

Time 32: inspection exposes the memory

c_{32}=c_1(0.98201379)^{31}=0.539327
o_{32}=\sigma(8-4)=0.982014,\quad h_{32}=o_{32}\tanh(c_{32})=0.483621

The exponent is 31: thirty normal readings plus the inspection step each apply the forget gate after the first cell. The healthy control starts and remains at c = h = 0 with these initial parameters.

Every forward time step, for both examples

6. Readout, probability, decision, and loss

\read=\v^\top h_T+\by,\qquad \prob=\sig(\read)

The readout converts the final hidden state into a logit r, then sigmoid converts the logit into a probability. The default decision threshold τ = 0.65 means “Check needed” when p ≥ τ. The threshold changes the decision, not the training loss.

\loss=-\target\log(\prob)-(1-\target)\log(1-\prob)

For a warning, y = 1 and the loss is −log(p). For a healthy control, y = 0 and the loss is −log(1−p). A confident wrong prediction has a large loss.

Only the final inspection is supervised here. Earlier hidden states are intermediate representations, not separate training predictions.

7. Backpropagation, step by step

A derivative asks how a small change affects the loss. Backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse order through the exact operations cached during the forward pass. It propagates gradients, not the original observations.

\frac{\sym{partial}{\partial}\loss}{\partial\params}\quad\text{measures the loss sensitivity to a parameter}

Backward step A · differentiate the final readout

For sigmoid followed by binary cross-entropy, the two derivatives simplify to p − y.

\delta_y=\prob-\target
\frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\v}=\delta_y h_T,\quad \frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\by}=\delta_y,\quad \sym{dh}{\bar h_T}=\delta_y\v

The readout gradient starts the hidden-state backward chain. For our warning example, p − y ≈ −0.053709 and the incoming final hidden gradient is approximately −0.429674.

Backward step B · collect the cell-state gradient

At time t, two routes can bring correction into cₜ: the current hidden output and the memory passed to the next cell. We call the total cell-state gradient Dₜ.

\Dtot=\dcfuture+\dh\had\gateo\had\left(1-\th^2(\ct)\right)

The future memory contribution is initialized to zero at the final step. At earlier steps, it is the dc propagated by the next cell. Both contributions must be added; dropping either loses part of the chain rule.

Backward step C · differentiate the output gate

\frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\gateo}=\dh\had\th(\ct)
\del{o}=\dh\had\th(\ct)\had\gateo\had(1-\gateo)

Multiply the hidden-state correction by the memory content it exposes, then by the sigmoid derivative. δₒ is the gradient with respect to the output gate’s preactivation, not its activation.

Backward step D · differentiate the forget gate

\frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\gatef}=\Dtot\had\cp
\del{f}=\Dtot\had\cp\had\gatef\had(1-\gatef)

The stored old content determines how much changing the forget gate matters. At the first cell, c₀ = 0, so the forget-gate derivative is zero. This local zero is correct: there was no old memory to retain.

Backward step E · differentiate the input gate

\frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\gatei}=\Dtot\had\cand
\del{i}=\Dtot\had\cand\had\gatei\had(1-\gatei)

The input gate controls the fraction of candidate content admitted. Its derivative teaches the model to write more or less.

Backward step F · differentiate the candidate

\frac{\partial\loss}{\partial\cand}=\Dtot\had\gatei
\del{g}=\Dtot\had\gatei\had(1-\cand^2)

The candidate’s tanh derivative teaches the content representation. A candidate can currently equal zero and still have a nonzero gradient: tanh′(0) = 1.

Backward step G · pass gradients to the previous states

\dcprev=\Dtot\had\gatef
\dhprev=\sum_{a\in\{f,i,g,o\}}\U{a}^{\top}\del{a}

The first equation is the direct memory route. The second collects all recurrent contributions through gate calculations. Repeat steps B–G from t = 32 down to t = 1.

Direct memory path versus the complete derivative
\left.\frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_t}\right|_{\mathrm{direct}}=\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}f_k

This product describes the green memory lane. The full recurrent derivative also contains indirect routes through h and the gates. The simulation’s backward pass includes those routes.

A fully substituted backward step: warning at t = 32

The correction reaching the first warning cell

Initially the LSTM’s recurrent U matrices are zero. Early dh values can therefore be zero even while the cell-state gradient is substantial. Plotting only dh would miss the memory route.

Every backward time step and gate derivative, for both examples

8. Accumulate gradients for shared parameters

Each affine gate uses input weights, recurrent weights, and a bias. Once its preactivation derivative δ is known, the local derivatives are outer products:

\nabla_{\W{a}}\loss=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\del{a}\xt^{\top}
\nabla_{\U{a}}\loss=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\del{a}\hp^{\top},\qquad \nabla_{\bias{a}}\loss=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\del{a}

The time index on each δ and input refers to the same step within the sum. Every use of the shared parameter contributes. The outer-product shapes match W (H × D) and U (H × H). We sum across time because there is one final loss per sequence; we do not divide these gradients by the number of time steps.

If an input feature is zero, that step contributes zero to its corresponding input weight. Other weights or biases can still receive nonzero derivatives.

Average the two examples

\grad=\frac{\nabla_{\params}L_{\mathrm{healthy}}+\nabla_{\params}L_{\mathrm{warning}}}{2}

Both examples must use the same old parameter values. We finish both forward/backward passes before applying the batch update. This is full-batch SGD with a batch size of two sequences.

9. Clip if necessary, then update

\lVert\grad\rVert_2=\sqrt{\sum_j G_j^2}
\alpha=\begin{cases}1,&\lVert\grad\rVert_2\le\clip\\ \clip/\lVert\grad\rVert_2,&\lVert\grad\rVert_2>\clip\end{cases}
G_{\mathrm{clipped}}=\alpha\grad,\qquad \params_{\mathrm{new}}=\params_{\mathrm{old}}-\eta\alpha\grad

A clipping limit of zero means clipping is disabled in this application, so α = 1. Clipping acts on the norm of the whole averaged gradient vector, not independently on every parameter. It preserves gradient direction while restricting update size.

A negative gradient increases a weight under gradient descent; a positive gradient decreases it. All new parameter values are computed using gradients from the same old model. Recomputing gradients after updating each individual weight would implement a different algorithm.

LSTM memory helps long-range credit assignment, but LSTMs can still have exploding gradients. Clipping and architectural memory paths address different aspects of training stability.

10. Walk through one complete epoch

This is the first epoch from the default initial LSTM, independent of whatever epoch your simulation is currently showing.

Epoch step 1 · prepare the two examples

Healthy sequence: 31 normal tokens followed by inspection; target 0. Warning sequence: a warning, 30 normal tokens, and inspection; target 1. Reset h₀ and c₀ for each example, but reuse the same parameter set.

Epoch step 2 · finish both forward passes

The tables above give every forward state. Readout probabilities and example losses are shown below. Neither example changes the parameters yet.

Epoch step 3 · finish both backward passes

Start with p − y for each example. Traverse every cell in reverse, differentiate each gate and state update, and sum all time-step contributions to each parameter. The expandable backward tables show this for both examples.

Epoch step 4 · average and clip

Epoch step 5 · apply every parameter update

The one-unit model has 22 scalar parameters: four components each have three input weights, one recurrent weight, and one bias, plus one readout weight and one readout bias. The table includes every parameter. Bracket indices use the same zero-based indexing as the simulation: input 0 is warning, input 1 is normal, input 2 is inspection.

Trace one update all the way from the early warning

Epoch step 6 · evaluate with the new weights

Evaluation runs new forward passes. A warning example’s confidence can decrease while the averaged loss improves: training also needs to reduce false warnings on the healthy example. We optimize the two-example objective, not warning probability alone.

What changed after this epoch?

All parameter gradients were considered. Parameters with a zero gradient remain unchanged. Other gate weights, biases, recurrent weights, and readout values move together. States and gate activations are recalculated from the new parameters; they are not directly updated by SGD.

11. Repeat epochs and measure convergence

A time step is one observation. An epoch processes the full training set once. Here each epoch processes two complete sequences and performs one averaged-gradient update.

The configurable controls have distinct roles:

SettingMeaning
Hidden unitsSize of each hidden and cell-state vector; changes the number of trainable parameters.
Learning rate ηMultiplier on the clipped gradient when updating weights.
Maximum epochsHard limit for the configured training run.
Loss targetStop when the average post-update loss is at or below the target.
Minimum loss changeDefines how small consecutive loss changes must be to count toward a plateau.
Plateau patienceNumber of consecutive small-change epochs before stopping above the target.
Clipping limit CMaximum averaged-gradient norm before rescaling; zero disables it.
Sequence gapTask setting that controls how far the precursor is from inspection.
Decision threshold τTask policy for converting probability into a check/no-check decision.

With defaults, the LSTM reaches the 0.08 loss target at epoch 78. The RNN reaches the 80-epoch limit above the target and misses the warning. A plateau above the target is not successful convergence. Different initialization and settings can change these outcomes.

12. Read the mechanisms correctly

Memory loss and vanishing gradients are separate. Forward memory loss asks whether the early evidence survives. Vanishing gradients asks whether a later loss can teach the early computation. A model can carry a value yet have a poor learning path.

Gates do not store separate memories. They control retaining, writing, and exposing. The candidate proposes content. The cell state holds internal memory.

A small hidden state need not mean forgotten memory. Our first LSTM cell has c ≈ 0.9467 but h ≈ 0.0133 because its output gate is mostly closed.

Near-one forget gates help; they do not guarantee perfect memory. Repeated factors below one still decay. Gates are learned and input-dependent.

Tanh-bounded states do not prevent exploding gradients. Unsaturated states with recurrent factors above one can amplify corrections. The exploding preset demonstrates this with the healthy control.

Training learns parameters, not the displayed gate numbers directly. The gate values, states, probabilities, losses, and gradients are results of computation.

The defaults are an explanatory initialization. The demo uses actual gradients and updates, but it is not evidence that all RNNs fail or that all LSTMs succeed on real battery data.
